paragraphs: Recognizing a three-dimensional object involves connecting its appearance from particular viewpoints with its identity. An earlier view-based model predicted units that respond preferentially to specific views, alongside units whose responses remain stable across views. Such response types were subsequently observed in the inferior temporal cortex of monkeys trained to recognize particular paperclip objects.

The earlier model left an important mechanistic question open: what information enters a view-tuned unit, and how is that unit organized internally? This paper proposes a model of those units. Its contribution is therefore to develop a previously unspecified component of the recognition account, connecting the idea of viewpoint sensitivity to a more concrete account of neuronal organization.

The proposed model is consistent with physiological measurements of individual cell responses. That agreement matters because a recognition theory must explain neuronal behavior as well as recognition performance. The stated result supports the plausibility of the proposed units within a view-based account, without establishing that physiological agreement uniquely identifies their biological implementation.
neurips-1996-3d-object-recognition-a-mod.tldr: The paper models the inputs and internal organization of viewpoint-sensitive recognition units in a way consistent with single-neuron responses.

paragraphs: A character recognizer can make systematic mistakes for a particular writer while still producing informative outputs. This paper builds on the idea that the complete output pattern remains characteristic of the input, even when the final recognition is wrong. Those patterns provide a basis for adapting an existing neural network to an individual user.

The proposed Output Adaptation Module takes the original network's output and maps it to a confidence vector appropriate for that user. It uses a simplified Resource Allocating Network that constructs radial basis functions online. Adaptation therefore adds a learned mapping at the output, with new basis functions supplying the components needed to represent a writer's particular corrections.

Applied to online handprinted character recognition, the module reduced test-set word error rate by an average of 45%. It created only 3 to 25 basis functions per writer in that test set. Together, these results show that a relatively small personalized output mapping can capture useful information in the recognizer's existing responses and substantially improve recognition for individual writers.
neurips-1996-a-constructive-rbf-network-.tldr: A small online adaptation module learns writer-specific corrections to a recognizer's outputs, reducing average test-set word error by 45%.

paragraphs: The paper presents a learning algorithm intended to produce Bayes-optimal predictions in large feed-forward neural networks. The target is predictive behavior that accounts for uncertainty through Bayesian reasoning. The authors describe this optimality as an expectation for the proposed algorithm, making the distinction between its intended behavior and its demonstrated results important.

Its central tool is a mean field method drawn from the statistical mechanics of disordered systems. Such an approach represents complicated interactions through an effective aggregate description. The paper derives the algorithm for a single-layer perceptron, providing a specific setting in which the proposed connection between statistical mechanics and neural-network prediction can be worked through.

The same algorithm also supplies a leave-one-out cross-validation test, which assesses predictions by considering examples withheld individually from learning. Simulations agree closely with the statistical-mechanics theory. This agreement supports the theoretical description in the examined setting, while the cross-validation result adds a way to assess predictions alongside producing them. The contribution thus links learning, theoretical analysis, and predictive checking within one framework.
neurips-1996-a-mean-field-algorithm-for-.tldr: A mean field algorithm targets Bayesian prediction in large neural networks and also yields a leave-one-out predictive check.

paragraphs: Wordspotting seeks to identify target words within speech, and this paper addresses one component of such a system: decoding the states of a hidden Markov model. The decoder handles the model's state-based representation of the speech sequence. The contribution concerns implementing that computation in hardware under a stringent electrical power requirement.

The central design specification is power dissipation on the scale of microwatts. This requirement motivates a continuous-time analog circuit implementation. The choice of computational medium is therefore part of the solution: the authors organize state decoding around circuit behavior that operates continuously, with the power target guiding the hardware architecture.

The paper characterizes a test chip containing a decoder for 10 words represented by 81 states. This provides a concrete implementation at a stated vocabulary and state count. Its significance lies in bringing a speech-recognition computation into a hardware design centered on very low power. The reported work concerns the state decoder as a component, so its scope is the operation of that chip within the broader wordspotting task.
neurips-1996-a-micropower-analog-vlsi-hm.tldr: The paper implements and characterizes a 10-word, 81-state analog HMM decoder designed around microwatt power dissipation.

paragraphs: The repeating rise and fall of a sound's amplitude carries timing information relevant to pitch. This paper presents a silicon model that uses synchronized neuronal spikes to extract a sound's fundamental frequency. Its organizing idea is that coordinated spike timing can make the periodic structure of an acoustic signal available to a physical circuit.

The biological motivation comes from neurons called choppers in the mammalian cochlear nucleus. These cells synchronize especially well with particular rates of amplitude modulation, depending on their own intrinsic chopping frequency. The model draws on this relationship between a cell's internal rhythm and the timing of changes in the incoming sound.

The implementation combines an artificial cochlea, an inner hair cell circuit, and a spiking neuron circuit. Together, these components form a hardware model connecting auditory input processing with spike-based timing. The contribution is a concrete circuit approach to a biologically motivated pitch-processing step: detecting modulation periodicity through synchrony. It places the temporal behavior of the neurons at the center of the computation.
neurips-1996-a-silicon-model-of-amplitud.tldr: A silicon auditory model uses synchronized spikes, inspired by cochlear-nucleus chopper cells, to extract a sound's fundamental frequency.

paragraphs: Interpolating between two data points requires choosing a route through the space that contains them. A short route may pass through regions that the data model considers unlikely. This paper defines interpolation using both the geometry of the route and a density model describing where data are concentrated.

The authors assign a cost to an entire path. One part favors travel through regions of high probability density, while another favors a small total path length. These competing goals make the desired interpolation a balance between remaining close to typical data and avoiding unnecessary detours. The model's density therefore influences the intermediate points along the transition.

From this path cost, the paper derives Euler–Lagrange equations describing extremal paths. Fixing the starting and ending points turns the computation into a boundary value problem. The authors show that interpolation can be performed efficiently in high dimensions for Gaussian, Dirichlet, and mixture models. The result supplies a principled way to make transitions depend on a learned or specified data distribution.
neurips-1996-a-variational-principle-for.tldr: The paper constructs interpolation paths that balance short length with travel through high-density regions of a data model.

paragraphs: Learning in a changing environment requires a model to keep adapting as new observations arrive. This paper proposes an online algorithm that extends the idea of learning how to learn. Its focus is adaptation of the learning process itself, with theoretical motivation for how that adaptation can support learning under changing conditions.

The algorithm relies only on gradient flow information: information about the directions in which learning updates move. It can be used to learn continuous functions or probability distributions without requiring an explicit loss function or access to the Hessian, which describes second-order curvature. Those requirements matter because an update direction can be available even when a fuller description of the optimization problem is unavailable.

The authors demonstrate the algorithm's efficiency on blind separation of acoustic signals in a nonstationary setting. Here, the separation problem changes during learning, giving the adaptive procedure a concrete tracking task. The demonstration connects the method's minimal information requirements with an application where continuing to adjust is essential to the learning problem.
neurips-1996-adaptive-on-line-learning-i.tldr: An adaptive online learning algorithm uses gradient flow alone and demonstrates efficiency on changing acoustic source-separation problems.

paragraphs: This paper identifies straight-line patterns in a two-dimensional lattice using a neural-network design inspired by orientation-selective visual cells. Such patterns matter in the application because cosmic muons can leave approximately linear arrangements of signals in a segmented particle detector. The task is to recognize these arrangements despite imperfections in the observations.

The authors construct a multilayer network with a fixed architecture that implements orientation selectivity. Different output elements correspond to different orientations, providing signals from which a selection decision can be made. The algorithm explicitly accounts for the lattice's granularity, noise, and detection inefficiencies, so its pattern representation reflects the discrete and imperfect nature of the detector data.

The method is applied to data from the ZEUS detector at HERA using a two-dimensional representation of the relevant calorimeter region. The authors report very good performance at identifying cosmic-muon patterns. They also identify the architecture as a promising candidate for fast recognition on parallel processing devices, linking the organization of the computation to its potential hardware execution.
neurips-1996-an-orientation-selective-ne.tldr: A fixed neural network with orientation-selective outputs detects cosmic-muon line patterns in noisy, segmented particle-detector data.

paragraphs: Temporal-difference learning estimates values from sequences of state transitions. This paper studies how the errors in those estimates change over learning, separating systematic error, or bias, from variability across estimates, or variance. The goal is an analytical account of learning curves that explains how repeated updates affect both components.

The analysis covers several temporal-difference value-estimation algorithms with offline updates over trials. It assumes absorbing Markov chains, whose trajectories can reach terminal states, and lookup-table representations, which store separate estimates for states. Within that setting, the authors calculate expressions for the evolution of bias and variance, making the relationship between updates and mean squared error explicit.

Examples across different chains illustrate distinct classes of learning-curve behavior. The analysis also shows how strongly those curves depend on step size and eligibility trace parameters. Step size controls the scale of updates, while eligibility traces govern how updates reach earlier states. The contribution is a way to understand parameter sensitivity through the changing structure of estimation error.
neurips-1996-analytical-mean-squared-err.tldr: The paper derives bias and variance learning curves for tabular temporal-difference methods, revealing sensitivity to step size and eligibility traces.

paragraphs: Optimal stopping asks when to stop a stochastic process rather than continue observing its evolution. This paper proposes an approximate solution for a discounted Markov-chain setting. The chain is assumed to be irreducible and aperiodic, conditions that restrict its long-run transition behavior and form part of the theoretical setting.

The algorithm represents a Q-function as a weighted combination of fixed basis functions. It updates those weights incrementally using simulated transitions from the underlying chain, following an iterative procedure similar to Q-learning. This representation lets the method express decision values through shared functions instead of requiring an independently adjustable value for every possible situation.

The paper outlines a proof of convergence with probability one and gives approximation-error bounds. These results establish theoretical support for combining a Q-learning-like update with arbitrary linear function approximators in this stopping problem. The treatment focuses on finite state spaces; the abstract states that continuous and unbounded extensions belong to a fuller treatment. The guarantee is therefore tied to the specified sequential decision setting.
neurips-1996-approximate-solutions-to-op.tldr: A Q-learning-like algorithm approximates optimal stopping values with fixed basis functions and comes with convergence and approximation-error results.

paragraphs: ARTEX is a self-organizing system for classifying image regions from their visual properties. Its architecture connects an image-processing stage with an incremental learning stage. This arrangement addresses both how to describe a region and how to learn useful classifications from descriptions that can be multidimensional and noisy.

The preprocessor combines filtering at multiple scales with competition, cooperation, and diffusion. These operations produce a vector describing boundaries and surfaces, especially texture and brightness. The resulting vector becomes the input to a system that incrementally learns mappings and their probabilities. Thus, the classifier works with a structured description of regional appearance and associates that description with learned probabilistic relationships.

The authors apply the architecture to synthetic aperture radar imagery and natural texture images, presenting both as difficult real-world classification problems. On natural textures, ARTEX outperforms a recent state-of-the-art system. That comparison supports the usefulness of combining the proposed visual preprocessing with incremental probabilistic learning for the tested texture-classification task. The radar application additionally demonstrates use with another type of image data.
neurips-1996-artex-a-self-organizing-arc.tldr: ARTEX combines multiscale image descriptions with incremental probabilistic learning and outperforms a contemporary system on natural-texture classification.

paragraphs: A neural code based on precise spike timing must remain reliable as neuromodulators change neuronal behavior. Cholinergic modulation creates a particular concern because it reduces spike-frequency adaptation, the tendency for firing to slow during continued stimulation. That change appears capable of shifting spike times and disrupting information carried by their timing.

The authors test this concern using whole-cell patch-clamp recordings from rat neocortical slices together with compartmental modeling. They examine responses to fluctuating inputs that resemble conditions in a living brain. The character of the input is central: the study asks whether timing survives modulation when the neuron receives physiologically realistic fluctuations.

Under those conditions, cholinergic modulation preserved spike timing. This finding supports the possibility that precise timing can remain a reliable component of neural coding despite changes in modulation. The authors interpret it as evidence that spike timing in vivo may be more resistant to neuromodulator changes than earlier physiological work suggested. The direct observation comes from the slice and modeling conditions, while the implication concerns robustness in the living brain.
neurips-1996-cholinergic-modulation-pres.tldr: Recordings and modeling show preserved spike timing under cholinergic modulation when neurons receive fluctuations resembling in vivo input.

paragraphs: An image can support several interpretations at the level of individual parts, even when its overall scene is readily understood. This paper treats that relationship between local ambiguity and global context as a central recognition problem. Global models can capture context, but the authors identify computational intractability as an obstacle for unconstrained recognition.

Their proposed alternative builds objects compositionally. Primitive elements are recursively combined under syntactic restrictions, producing tree-structured representations of objects and object groupings. The restrictions govern which combinations are permitted. This gives the model a structured way to connect small visual elements with larger interpretations at successive levels of a hierarchy.

The model carries multiple candidate interpretations upward instead of committing immediately to one local explanation. A Bayesian cost, equivalently expressed through minimum description length, later resolves those alternatives. In plain terms, the system judges competing explanations using a shared probabilistic or description-length criterion once broader context is available. The contribution is an architecture for preserving useful ambiguity while organizing the construction and evaluation of whole-object interpretations.
neurips-1996-compositionality-mdl-priors.tldr: A compositional vision model carries multiple interpretations through a hierarchy and resolves them with a Bayesian minimum-description-length criterion.

paragraphs: Hidden variables can explain why observed quantities vary together. This paper proposes a belief-network unit that allows those hidden variables to take real values, expanding the kinds of latent structure the network can represent. The aim is to combine useful stochastic behavior with a simple construction for individual units.

Each unit adds zero-mean Gaussian noise to its input and then passes the result through a sigmoidal squashing function. This order of operations produces a range of behaviors, including effectively deterministic outputs, binary stochastic outputs, and continuous stochastic outputs. A single unit design can therefore express different forms of hidden-variable behavior within the network framework.

The paper shows how slice sampling can support inference and learning in top-down networks built from these units. Inference concerns hidden-variable values associated with observations, while learning adjusts the model to the data. Demonstrations on two simple problems show learning with the proposed construction. The contribution brings together a flexible stochastic unit and a sampling method that makes networks of those units usable for latent-structure modeling.
neurips-1996-continuous-sigmoidal-belief.tldr: Adding Gaussian noise before a sigmoid creates flexible belief-network units that can be trained and used for inference with slice sampling.

paragraphs: Noisy time-series data create two connected uncertainties: the underlying state of the process is hidden, and the model describing that process may also be unknown. This paper treats prediction, estimation, and smoothing through that joint problem. It explicitly includes system noise when modeling how the observations are generated.

The authors discuss maximum-likelihood and Kalman frameworks that estimate both model parameters and system states. After reviewing established linear methods, they propose extensions using dual Kalman filters and forward-backward filters that can be applied to neural networks. The dual viewpoint keeps parameter learning and state estimation connected, since each depends on the other when observations are noisy.

The methods are compared in simulations involving several noisy time series, and the paper includes nonlinear speech-noise reduction as an application. These examples place the proposed extensions in concrete signal-processing settings. The contribution is a framework for carrying uncertainty about both dynamics and state into nonlinear modeling, with prediction and reconstruction treated as related uses of the same underlying process model.
neurips-1996-dual-kalman-filtering-metho.tldr: The paper extends dual and forward-backward filtering to neural-network models that jointly estimate noisy system states and model parameters.

paragraphs: Understanding a neural network's training requires describing how learning unfolds across successive updates. This paper introduces a method for calculating that training process with results directly tied to the actual number of training steps. The approach makes the passage from one stage of learning to another an explicit object of analysis.

The method avoids sophisticated machinery such as the replica trick. Its stated results include a maximal learning rate, an exact description of early stopping, and the necessary number of training steps. These are closely related questions: the rate controls update size, stopping selects a point along the process, and the step count describes how long training must proceed.

Connecting those quantities to the training trajectory gives practical choices a common analytical setting. Early stopping, in particular, becomes something that can be described through the calculated dynamics. The paper presents these results as examples of what the method can address and indicates that further training questions can be studied through the same approach.
neurips-1996-dynamics-of-training-b5bbba.tldr: A method for calculating neural-network training dynamics links learning-rate limits, early stopping, and required training duration to actual update counts.

paragraphs: Pruning reduces a neural network's size by removing weights. Optimal Brain Damage chooses weights using an approximation to the increase in the cost function caused by removing them. That approximation assumes training has reached a local minimum, creating a conflict with early stopping, which deliberately ends learning before that point.

The paper shows that Optimal Brain Damage estimates the cost increase incorrectly when the network is away from a local minimum. It then extends the method to handle networks stopped early. The resulting approach, Early Brain Damage, makes the pruning calculation compatible with the state in which early stopping leaves the network.

Early Brain Damage also permits previously pruned weights to be revived, so a removal decision need not remain permanent. The authors demonstrate improvements on three publicly available datasets. The central contribution is to resolve a specific mismatch between a pruning approximation and a training procedure. By adapting the cost estimate to early stopping, the method supports using those two ways of controlling a network together.
neurips-1996-early-brain-damage-335794a0.tldr: Early Brain Damage corrects pruning estimates for networks stopped before a local minimum and allows removed weights to be restored.

paragraphs: Learning a Bayesian belief network requires estimating probabilistic relationships among variables. This paper proposes using artificial neural networks for those probability estimates. The motivation is to avoid choosing a particular distributional form in advance for the relationships that the belief network is intended to capture.

Neural-network estimators provide the probability information used by the learning method. This gives the approach potential applicability to domains containing both discrete and continuous variables with arbitrarily shaped distributions. The flexibility concerns how relationships are represented probabilistically, allowing the data-driven estimators to take on a role that would otherwise depend on prior distributional assumptions.

The authors compare the method with the learning procedure of Cooper and Herskovits. Their experiments find comparable learning accuracy, while the neural-estimator approach is slower. The result identifies a concrete tradeoff: greater flexibility in the probability-estimation scheme comes with additional learning time in the reported comparison. The contribution is a way to connect neural probability estimation with belief-network learning while exposing that computational cost.
neurips-1996-learning-bayesian-belief-ne.tldr: Neural probability estimators enable flexible Bayesian belief-network learning, with comparable accuracy but slower learning than the compared method.

paragraphs: A learner that can request additional examples must decide which queries are most useful. This paper proposes selecting them to reduce estimated squared bias, the systematic component of prediction error. The criterion aims to improve the learner by directing queries toward the error that its current predictions are expected to make consistently.

This emphasis differs from a variance-focused exploration criterion, which targets uncertainty or variability in the learner's estimates. The proposed method uses estimated bias as its sole query-selection objective. Its importance lies in treating systematic prediction error as actionable information for deciding what to learn next, rather than assuming that reducing variability is sufficient.

Experiments use locally weighted regression on two simple problems. In those settings, the bias-focused approach outperforms the variance-focused alternative, including when noise is present. The finding shows that noisy observations do not automatically make variance reduction the better querying strategy. Within the tested problems, directing queries toward systematic error produces the stronger learning result, motivating attention to bias when designing exploration criteria.
neurips-1996-minimizing-statistical-bias.tldr: Selecting queries to reduce estimated squared bias beats variance-focused exploration on two locally weighted regression problems, even with noise.

paragraphs: A generalization bound can be mathematically valid yet give little information about how well a network actually learns. This paper studies that gap for multilayer perceptrons with hard-threshold hidden units. It analyzes worst-case learning curves within a particular class of input probability distributions, giving the comparison a specified distributional setting.

The analysis takes a large-system limit in which sample size is scaled by the number of connections to the first hidden layer. In the regime described, the true learning curve improves approximately inversely with the scaled sample size, while the VC-dimension bound remains at the trivial error bound of one. The VC-entropy bound also stays trivial across a stated range.

The authors additionally derive bounds that follow the true learning curve using a formalism based on the density of error patterns. This shows that the loose VC results reflect the information captured by those bounds, rather than the learning behavior itself. The contribution is both a demonstrated gap and an alternative route to more informative guarantees in the analyzed setting.
neurips-1996-mlp-can-provably-generalize.tldr: For a specified class of threshold networks and input distributions, actual learning substantially outpaces VC bounds, while error-pattern-based bounds track it.

paragraphs: Predicting future returns for several stocks raises an architectural question: how much should their predictors share? This paper considers a separate neural network for each stock, a common network across stocks, and intermediate designs. It frames each stock's prediction problem as a distinct task within a broader learning system.

The intermediate architectures share some layers while keeping others specific to individual stocks. Shared parameters allow the tasks to use common learned structure, while unshared parameters preserve stock-specific modeling. This makes the allocation of shared and individual components the central design choice. In this formulation, stock selection becomes an application of multi-task learning.

In experiments with Canadian stocks, the authors report yearly returns more than 14% above various benchmarks. That is the stated outcome of their experimental series, connecting the modeling question to financial decisions based on predicted returns. The paper's methodological contribution is the exploration of partial parameter sharing as an alternative between fully separate predictors and a single shared predictor for every stock.
neurips-1996-multi-task-learning-for-sto.tldr: The paper explores shared and stock-specific neural-network layers, reporting yearly returns more than 14% above various benchmarks in Canadian-stock experiments.

paragraphs: Many classification problems have categories with a meaningful order, and examples may lack some input information. This paper addresses both features together. The ordering gives the output classes structure, while incompleteness affects the evidence available for learning from earlier cases and making predictions for new ones.

The authors propose a nonlinear ordinal classification model. Calling the model ordinal means that the classes' relative order is part of the problem formulation; allowing nonlinearity gives the relationship between inputs and ordered outcomes additional flexibility. Predictive, simulation-based procedures support both training on incomplete historical examples and classifying future examples that are also incomplete.

The techniques are illustrated through prognosis for patients who have suffered severe head injuries. This application brings together ordered outcomes and partial observations in a concrete prediction task. The contribution is a modeling approach that accommodates those two properties within the same learning and prediction process. Its treatment of incomplete examples extends across both stages, so missing information is addressed when constructing the model and when using it.
neurips-1996-ordered-classes-and-incompl.tldr: A nonlinear ordinal model uses simulation-based prediction to learn from and classify incomplete examples, illustrated with severe-head-injury prognosis.

paragraphs: Source separation seeks to recover underlying signals from their mixtures. This paper couples that task with density estimation, using the local geometry of the observed distribution as information about how sources are combined. The underlying sources are assumed to be statistically independent, providing the structure the separation method aims to recover.

The authors modify a self-organizing map to perform nonparametric histogram density estimation through purely digital learning rules. Nonparametric separation allows the approach to handle nonlinear mixtures. They also introduce anisotropic coupling, meaning that interactions depend on direction, to align the network locally with contours associated with the independent components.

The resulting approach provides an exact condition for verifying source separation without requiring a prior distribution for the sources. That distinction matters: independence supplies an assumption about the relationship between sources, while their individual distributional shapes need not be prescribed. The contribution connects geometric organization, density estimation, and separation in one method, with a stated verification criterion for judging whether the desired separation has been achieved.
neurips-1996-source-separation-and-densi.tldr: A modified self-organizing map uses distribution geometry to separate nonlinear mixtures of independent sources and provides an exact separation check.

paragraphs: A natural-language query must be converted into something a retrieval system can execute. This paper investigates how single-neuron learning algorithms can improve that process. The focus is the connection between a user's initial wording, the query submitted to an existing retrieval system, and the resulting treatment of documents.

The proposed retrieval process expands the initial query using statistical and learning techniques, then translates it into the target system's query syntax. The expanded query is used for document ranking and binary classification. These are related outputs: ranking orders documents, while binary classification assigns them to one of two categories. Learning therefore participates in a pipeline that supports both forms of retrieval decision.

Experiments suggest that Kivinen and Warmuth's Exponentiated Gradient Descent performs significantly better than previous approaches. The reported finding favors that learning algorithm within the investigated retrieval setting. The contribution is to show how a relatively simple learned component can improve the transformation and use of natural-language queries in a working text-retrieval process.
neurips-1996-text-based-information-retr.tldr: A query-expansion and retrieval pipeline using Exponentiated Gradient Descent shows significantly better experimental performance than previous approaches.

paragraphs: Maximizing and minimizing information can sound like opposing goals. This paper combines them by applying them at different levels of a neural network's hidden representation. It defines collective information for the hidden units together and individual information for units considered separately, allowing the two objectives to play distinct roles.

The method maximizes collective information while minimizing individual information. The authors argue that this can produce simpler networks with fewer connections and hidden units. They expect that simplification to support better generalization and more interpretable internal representations. The key idea is that preserving useful information across the group can coexist with reducing the information attributed to individual components.

The method is applied to learning the maximum onset principle in an artificial language. In that task, the results show that individual information minimization is compatible with collective information maximization. Experiments also confirm improved generalization through substantial suppression of over-training. The findings support the proposed compatibility and connect the information objectives to a demonstrated improvement in learning behavior.
neurips-1996-unification-of-information-.tldr: Maximizing collective hidden-unit information while minimizing individual information produces simpler networks and improves generalization on an artificial-language task.
